name: Sclera tattoo (eyeball tattooing)

lead: Scleral tattooing injects pigment into the white of the eye to color it permanently. It came out of body-modification culture in the mid-2000s, and people choose it for a striking colored-eye look that shows immediately.

Ink is placed under the conjunctiva or into the layers of the sclera, where it spreads and stays. It is a cosmetic modification rather than a treatment, and the published literature consists of case reports of complications.

paras: It is performed by body-modification practitioners as a one-off procedure and the colour is permanent. The result is visible as soon as swelling settles.

Case reports describe uveitis, endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, vision loss and other reactions, including ink entering the eye. Ontario, Saskatchewan, Indiana and Oklahoma have restricted or banned it, according to Wikipedia.

angle.text: Pigment injected into the white of the eye gives a permanent colour change that shows straight away. The published information is mostly case reports of vision-threatening complications.

lead: Scleral tattooing, also called eyeball tattooing or conjunctival tattooing, is a body modification in which pigment is injected under the conjunctiva into the sclera, the white of the eye, so that the whites take on a permanent color such as blue, black, red or purple [1]. People choose it as a striking aesthetic statement: it changes the most visible contrast in the eye, turning the whites into a color that frames the iris and gives the face a distinctive, stylized look.

The modern practice is credited to Canadian body-modification figure Shannon Larratt and practitioner Howie 'Luna Cobra' Rollins in 2007. Larratt had edited a photo around 2003 to give himself blue eyes like the Fremen in Dune and asked Rollins to find a way to make that permanent [1]. Wikipedia reports no documented cosmetic use before the early 21st century, apart from occasional 1940s reports of dotting the sclera in eye-movement experiments [1].

Published literature on the procedure consists of case reports and small series of complications, including intraocular ink injection with inflammation, secondary glaucoma, cataract, retinal detachment and retinal necrosis, a sarcoid-type reaction, and unexpected lacrimal gland infiltration [2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]. Ontario, Saskatchewan, Oklahoma and Indiana have restricted or banned the procedure [1].

paras: The procedure delivers dye between two layers of the eye, the conjunctiva and sclera, after which the pigment spreads [1]. Practitioners originally experimented with covering a needle in ink and puncturing the eye, which Rollins judged unsuccessful, before injecting blue dye into the sclera, a method similar to one used by surgeons for eye implants [1].

A related practice is placing thin platinum jewelry under the conjunctiva; Larratt's wife Rachel had a surgeon inject saline to create a fluid pocket before the jewelry was inserted. The Ontario and Saskatchewan bans cover this eye jewelry as well [1].

Around 2003 Larratt altered a photo of himself to resemble the blue-eyed Fremen of Dune. After Rollins agreed to attempt a permanent version if Larratt found two other volunteers, Larratt underwent the procedure in 2007 [1]. In a 2007 BMEzine article Larratt described minor pain, bruising, discomfort and mild blistering as aftereffects, warned of risks including blindness, said it should only be done by a professional, and noted long-term effects had not been measured [1].

The practice spread through the body-modification community, and by 2015 ophthalmology journals were describing eyeball tattooing as an emerging trend and calling it a new form of extreme body modification that first emerged in 2007 [4][8]. Wikipedia notes that two widely reported cases, those of Canadian Catt Gallinger (2017) and Briton Anaya-Nicole Parke-Peterson, drew international media coverage and calls for clearer regulation and training, though those sections of the article lack citations [1].

Published case reports describe a range of outcomes. A 21-year-old woman developed ocular inflammation, secondary glaucoma and cataract after intraocular dye injection, and required surgery and laser iridotomy [2]. A 25-year-old woman whose procedure inadvertently penetrated the globe developed severe uveitis, capsular lens opacity and secondary glaucoma [3]. A 28-year-old man developed conjunctival edema and anterior uveitis after tattooing [4]. A 2015 case described ocular penetration and intraocular pigment deposition [5].

A 40-year-old man had dye injected into the suprachoroidal space and was followed for 8 months without inflammatory sequelae, which the authors note shows some patients may tolerate the dye surprisingly well [6]. A 2021 case report describes a man who received inadvertent intraocular injection and later developed delayed granulomatous uveitis, and other reports describe retinal detachment and retinal necrosis, a sarcoid reaction, and blue tears after infiltration of the lacrimal gland [10][11][12][7].

Two cases of improvised scleral tattoos made in prison with pen ink and insulin needles had minimal complications managed with topical medication, according to a 2021 report that also reviews the literature on the dangers of the practice [8]. Ophthalmology authors state that ophthalmologists should be aware of the presentation and management of such cases [2][8].

Per Wikipedia, the Oklahoma Senate passed a bill in 2009 to ban the procedure with the support of the Oklahoma Academy of Ophthalmology, Ontario banned it in February 2017, Indiana banned it in 2018 with a fine of $10,000, and Saskatchewan banned it in January 2020 [1].
No systematic studies or trials were found. The evidence consists of published case reports and small series on complications [2][3][4][5][6][8][9][10][11][12][7][8].

lore.intro: Claims about the safety and permanence of scleral tattooing come mainly from body-modification practitioners and from ophthalmology case reports.

claims.claim: Aftereffects are mild and the result is safe in a professional's hands
Some people tolerate the dye with no inflammation
Improvised methods such as pen ink are a workable alternative
